\title{Physics-guided machine-learning prediction of spontaneous energy localization in a sine-Gordon pendulum ring}

% TODO-AUTHORS: Adrian Mittal is listed alone for now. Decide the coauthors (and their
% affiliations and order) before posting, and update the affiliation below (the one used
% in Ref. [mittal2026jand] is kept as a placeholder).
\author{Adrian Mittal\\[2pt]
{\small International Research Institute of North Carolina, Sanford, NC 27330}}
% TODO-AUTHORS: add a contact e-mail if wanted.

\date{}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
In a ring of torsionally coupled pendulums with a weak global coupling, a nearly uniform swing is destabilized by a type-III instability and, after several swing periods, concentrates its energy on a few pendulums. In earlier work we predicted where this hotspot forms from early-time data, first by spatial smoothing and then with a convolutional and recurrent neural network. Here we revisit the problem starting from the physics of the instability. The Floquet growth spectrum of the uniform swing shows that only a handful of the longest ring modes grow, which accounts for the optimal smoothing width found before. The site is fixed by the initial state, so prediction is limited by measurement precision rather than by chaos. Letting the spectrum guide the design, and testing every choice by ablation, we replace the recurrent network with a small convolutional network built around the ring's symmetry. With a thousandth of the parameters, it halves the error of our rebuild of the earlier network, which falls short of the accuracy originally reported, and outperforms that rebuild with 60 times less training data. Much of the remaining error belongs to the target itself: the first pendulum to cross an energy threshold jitters within a swing, whereas the hump of energy that forms is located within one pendulum in 99.4\% of runs. We close with the limits that sensor noise, parameter errors, impurities and damping set in a real chain.
\end{abstract}

% ===========================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Dynamic energy localization, whereby a significant portion of a nonlinear system's energy becomes concentrated on a small part of it, is observed in many nonlinear oscillating systems \cite{sievers1988intrinsic,campbell2004localizing,flach2008discrete}, from micromechanical oscillator arrays \cite{sato2006colloquium} to large structures such as bridges \cite{green2006failure,ARIOLI2015901} and transmission lines \cite{zhang2017wind}. Because such ``hotspots'' often precede mechanical failure, predicting where they form is of practical as well as fundamental interest. A well-known pathway to localization is the modulational instability of a plane-wave mode \cite{kivshar1993creation,dauxois1993energy,extreme}. Of the three classes of instability distinguished by the wavenumber of the fastest-growing perturbation \cite{cross1993pattern}, type III often leads to catastrophic localization \cite{english2003modulational,thakur2007driven,cuevas2009discrete}. Since the instability is seeded by noise, where the energy localizes depends sensitively on the initial conditions.

In a previous paper \cite{mittal2026jand} we studied this problem numerically in the discrete sine-Gordon model \cite{cuevas2014sine}, realized as a ring of torsionally coupled pendulums with a weak global coupling that selects an instability of type III. Smoothing the early energy profile with a box-car of about 17 pendulums substantially improved predictions of the localization site, suggesting that the instability is sensitive to energetic clusters rather than to single pendulums. We then reported that a convolutional neural network combined with a bidirectional long short-term memory network \cite{Hochreiter1997} (CNN-BiLSTM) located the site within $\pm1$ pendulum in 94.4\% of test cases. We concluded that the network had found features beyond energy clusters, and that a future study should aim at teasing them out.

The present paper is that study. Rather than treat the predictor as a black box, we begin with the linear stability of the uniform swing, its Floquet growth spectrum, and ask what it implies for each design question: what to measure, what architecture to use, and how to train it. For each question we stated a hypothesis before running the experiment, grounded in the spectrum wherever the physics had something to say, and tested it with an ablation, a controlled comparison that could refute it, in the spirit of physics-informed machine learning \cite{karniadakis2021physics}. We also wanted a predictor that is efficient and easy to implement, small enough to train in minutes on a laptop and fed with measurements that a real chain could provide. We report the choices that did not pay off alongside those that did.

Three findings stand out. First, only a handful of the longest ring modes are unstable, and this explains the smoothing width of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}. Second, a network built around the ring's symmetry needs no recurrent layer, and with a thousandth of the parameters it halves the error of our rebuild of the CNN-BiLSTM. Third, much of the remaining error belongs to the label, because the first pendulum to cross an energy threshold jitters within a swing; defined at the scale of the hump of energy that forms, the site becomes almost fully predictable.

One caveat applies throughout. The training code of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} is not available to us, and our rebuild of that network from its published description reaches 60.4\% within $\pm1$ rather than 94.4\% (Sec.~\ref{sec:repro}). We therefore compare the two networks, which we call \emph{v1} and \emph{v2}, on the same test runs using this rebuild, and compare both with physics baselines that do not depend on it. Section~\ref{sec:methods} introduces the model, its growth spectrum and our methods, Sec.~\ref{sec:results} presents the results, Sec.~\ref{sec:repro} discusses the reproduction of v1, and Sec.~\ref{sec:conclusions} concludes.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Methods}
\label{sec:methods}

\subsection{The pendulum ring}

We consider the same system as in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}: a ring of $N$ pendulums with torsional nearest-neighbour coupling and a global coupling to the chain average. In dimensionless time $\tau=\omega_0 t$, the angles obey
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:eom}
\ddot\theta_n = -\sin\theta_n + \gt\,(\theta_{n+1}+\theta_{n-1}-2\theta_n) + \htl\,(\bar\theta-\theta_n),
\end{equation}
where $\bar\theta$ is the mean angle over the ring, indices are taken modulo $N$, and the dot denotes $d/d\tau$. We use $N=100$, $\gt=0.75$ and $\htl=0.5$.\footnote{Section~2.1 of the journal version of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} prints $\htl=0.05$, a typographical error: Sec.~2.3 there and the simulation code use $\htl=0.5$, the value that gives the instability threshold near $A=1.59$ reported there (Sec.~\ref{sec:floquet}).} Each run starts at rest with $\theta_n(0)=A+\eta_n$, where the amplitude $A\sim\mathcal{U}(1.65,1.85)$ is drawn once per run and the offsets $\eta_n\sim\mathcal{U}(-0.025,0.025)$ independently for every pendulum. The energy of site $n$ is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:energy}
E_n = \tfrac12\dot\theta_n^2 + (1-\cos\theta_n) + \tfrac{\gt}{2}(\theta_{n+1}-\theta_n)^2 + \tfrac{\htl}{2}(\theta_n-\bar\theta)^2 ,
\end{equation}
which assigns to each pendulum the spring to its right-hand neighbour, as in the code of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}; the total energy $\Etot=\sum_n E_n$ is conserved. After swinging almost uniformly for several tens of time units, about 57 on average, the ring suddenly concentrates its energy, and one pendulum holds more than 10\% of the total, ten times its equipartition share. For pendulums 20~cm long this happens about 8~s after release. We ask how well the early behaviour of the ring predicts which pendulum this will be.

\subsection{Linear stability of the uniform swing}
\label{sec:floquet}

Without offsets, every pendulum follows the same swing $\Theta(\tau)$, with $\ddot\Theta=-\sin\Theta$, $\Theta(0)=A$ and $\dot\Theta(0)=0$, whose period is $T(A)=4\mathcal{K}\!\left(\sin^2(A/2)\right)$, $\mathcal{K}$ being the complete elliptic integral of the first kind. Writing $\theta_n=\Theta+\delta\theta_n$ and expanding the perturbation in ring modes, $\delta\theta_n=\sum_m a_m(\tau)\,e^{2\pi i mn/N}$, we linearize Eq.~(\ref{eq:eom}) and obtain for every mode $m\ge1$ a Hill equation \cite{magnus1966hill},
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:hill}
\ddot a_m + \left[\cos\Theta(\tau) + \htl + 4\gt\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi m}{N}\right)\right] a_m = 0 ,
\end{equation}
whose coefficient is periodic with period $T(A)$. The global term adds the same stiffness $\htl$ to every mode except the uniform one, which is the swing itself; as discussed in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, this shift is what selects an instability of type III. Integrating Eq.~(\ref{eq:hill}) over one period gives the $2\times2$ monodromy matrix $M_m(A)$, whose eigenvalue of largest modulus, $\mu_m$, defines the growth rate $\sigma_m(A)=\ln|\mu_m(A)|/T(A)$; mode $m$ grows when $\sigma_m>0$.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig1_spectrum.pdf}
  \caption{Floquet growth spectrum of the uniform swing, Eq.~(\ref{eq:hill}). (a)~Growth rate $\sigma_m$ of ring mode $m$ (wavelength $100/m$ pendulums) against the swing amplitude $A$; the swing becomes unstable at $A_c=1.577$, and the bar marks the amplitudes in the data. (b)~At $A=1.75$ only modes $m=1$--$5$ grow; the labels give the $e$-folding time of each mode.}
  \label{fig:spectrum}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:spectrum} shows the resulting spectrum. The uniform swing becomes unstable at $A_c=1.577$, consistent with the vertical asymptote of the localization time near $A=1.59$ found numerically in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}. As the amplitude increases, more long waves become unstable, but only a few do in the range used here: at $A=1.75$ only the five longest waves grow, with wavelengths of 100, 50, 33, 25 and 20 pendulums. The fastest grows by a factor of $e$ every 8.4 time units, so during the first 4.5 time units after release, the observation window of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, the perturbation grows by less than a factor of two.

Three expectations follow, and they guide everything below. First, since the growing modes are the longest waves of the ring, the eventual site should be a property of the whole ring rather than of a local neighbourhood. Second, since so little growth occurs in the observation window, a predictor must essentially read the initial perturbation and project it onto the growing modes, rather than watch the hotspot form. Third, little else happens in time during that window: a small-amplitude estimate of the largest group velocity gives about half a pendulum per time unit, so a disturbance moves by only about two pendulums. Moreover, since the ring is released from rest, the initial angles $\theta_n(0)$ are its complete state, and every later frame is a function of them.

\subsection{Simulation, labels and metrics}
\label{sec:pools}

Training some 600 networks requires far more simulated runs than Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} did, so we replaced its run-by-run \texttt{odeint} integration \cite{virtanen2020scipy} with a fourth-order Runge--Kutta scheme \cite{press1992numerical} that integrates thousands of runs at once (step $\Delta\tau=0.05$, samples every 0.5 time units, as before). On 1,000 test runs it gives exactly the same localization site and time as the simulation code of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, about 100 times faster. Since the simulation is deterministic, we store only the initial angles of each run and regenerate any model input from them. Models are trained on up to 100,000 runs, the first 60,000 matching the training budget of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}; a validation pool of 20,000 runs serves for every model choice, and a test pool of 20,000 runs only for the numbers we report. The pools are generated with different random seeds, so no run appears in two of them, and inputs are standardized with statistics of the training pool alone.

Following Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, a run localizes at the first sample at which one site holds more than 10\% of the total energy, $\max_n E_n>0.1\,\Etot$, and its label is that site. We call this the \emph{first-crossing label} and use it for every comparison with v1; two smoother labels are introduced in Sec.~\ref{sec:target}. Distances are measured around the ring, $d(n,n')=\min(|n-n'|,\,N-|n-n'|)$. Accuracy within $\pm1$, the metric of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, was chosen there because the localized energy spans several pendulums, a point that Sec.~\ref{sec:target} bears out; it also partly rewards a convention, since in 21\% of runs which pendulum crosses first depends on how the spring energy in Eq.~(\ref{eq:energy}) is shared between neighbours. We therefore also report the mean distance between predicted and true site, the accuracy within $\pm3$, and the share of runs more than 10 sites off, which we call far misses. The test pool resolves an accuracy to about $\pm0.3\%$.

\subsection{Predictors and protocol}
\label{sec:predictors}

We compare the networks with three physics baselines. The \emph{box-car} predictor of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} picks the site where a moving average of the site energy peaks, with the width and the time of the snapshot chosen on the validation pool. The \emph{Floquet filter} needs no training at all: it evolves the mean-subtracted initial angles through the linearized dynamics for six swing periods, multiplying each ring mode by its response computed from $M_m(A)$ at the run's estimated amplitude, and picks the site where the result peaks. The \emph{linear ring filter} is the simplest trained model that respects the ring, a multinomial logistic regression whose score at each site is a circular convolution of the initial angles over the whole ring, with amplitude-dependent weights (200 parameters); it is convex, and we fit it to its global optimum with L-BFGS \cite{liu1989limited}. We rebuilt v1 in PyTorch \cite{paszke2019pytorch} from Sec.~2.3 and the Appendix of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, with the layers, inputs, loss, optimizer and early stopping described there (26,499,205 parameters; Appendix~\ref{app:training}).

The study proceeded question by question. We first compared architectures, with v1's inputs, then the inputs, the loss and the optimizer, changing one choice at a time; finally we combined the best choices and removed them again one at a time to see which mattered. Inputs, losses and optimizers were compared in shorter screening runs with three training seeds (random initializations of the network), the final model with five. Every network was trained on one laptop (an Apple M3 Pro, on its built-in GPU); training details are given in Appendix~\ref{app:training}.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{What the growth spectrum explains}
\label{sec:physics}

Let us first return to the box-car smoothing of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, whose best width, 17 pendulums, was found empirically. A box-car of width $K$ first cancels the ring mode $m=N/K$; a wider box-car also suppresses longer waves, and a narrower one lets shorter ones through. The best width should therefore cancel the first stable mode, $m_c$, while keeping all the growing ones, which gives $K^*=N/m_c$, or $100/6\approx17$ at $A=1.75$, where modes 1--5 grow. Figure~\ref{fig:physics}(a) shows that this prediction matches the best width measured at seven amplitudes, from just above threshold to $A=1.90$. The energetic clusters identified in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} thus appear to be the growing long waves, seen through a low-pass filter.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig2_physics.pdf}
  \caption{(a)~The best box-car width (dots, with 16--84\% bootstrap ranges; 2,000 runs per amplitude) follows the Floquet band edge $K^*=N/m_c$ (line), where $m_c$ is the first stable mode; the empirical optimum of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} lies on it. (b)~Share of labels moved by more than one or three sites when white noise of the given size is added to the initial angles; diamonds give the share moved by more than one site when a $10^{-3}$~rad error is placed only in the growing or only in the stable modes. (c)~Share of labels moved by more than three sites when the initial perturbation keeps only the modes $m\le M$, or loses the growing ones.}
  \label{fig:physics}
\end{figure}

Since the localization process is noise-activated, one may ask next whether chaos limits how well it can be predicted. Figure~\ref{fig:physics}(b) shows that it does not. Perturbing the initial angles by $10^{-6}$~rad never changes the label, and neither does halving the integration step, so the label is a deterministic function of the initial state and the best possible accuracy is close to 100\%. What limits prediction is how precisely that state is known: an error of $10^{-3}$~rad on every pendulum moves a quarter of the labels by more than one site, and placed only in the growing modes, it moves half of them. Conversely [Fig.~\ref{fig:physics}(c)], deleting every initial mode except the growing ones keeps the site within $\pm3$ in 91\% of runs, whereas deleting the growing modes makes the site random. The coarse answer thus lives in about ten numbers, the amplitudes and phases of the five growing modes, while local detail decides the last site or two.

The physics alone already gets far (Table~\ref{tab:headline}). The best box-car reaches a mean distance of 5.07 sites, close to the 5.4 reported in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}. The Floquet filter, which simply grows the measured initial perturbation and has no trained parameters, matches the mean distance of the rebuilt v1 (3.12 against 3.14), although it is less often within $\pm1$. The 200-parameter linear ring filter beats the rebuilt v1 on every metric. These baselines set the bar that any network has to clear.

\subsection{What to measure}
\label{sec:inputs}

The v1 network was given the site energies at ten times, $\tau=0,0.5,\dots,4.5$, together with the initial angles $\theta_n(0)$, copied into every frame as static context. Energies were the natural input there, since both the box-car analysis and the label of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} are stated in terms of energy. The growth spectrum suggests two alternatives, however: angles instead of energies, and the angles at the time of each frame rather than only at release. The energy of Eq.~(\ref{eq:energy}) is computed from the angles, the velocities and the coupling constants, so it holds no information that these lack; at release, to first order in the offsets, $E_n(0)$ is simply a rescaled copy of $\theta_n(0)$. It is also expensive to measure, since velocities call for a gyroscope on every pendulum or noisy differencing of video frames, whereas a single camera can track every angle. And since the ring starts at rest, $\theta_n(0)$ alone is already the complete state. We therefore expected the initial angles alone to match v1's inputs, and frames of angles to do at least as well.

Both expectations held. In screening runs, ten angle frames gave a mean distance of 1.56, the initial angles alone 1.66, and v1's inputs 1.75. In noise-free data the later frames carry no new information, but they make the same information easier to learn, and on the cleaner labels of Sec.~\ref{sec:target} they are clearly worth having. Angles do have one weakness. If the observation starts at an unknown point in the swing, they need about a full swing of frames to do as well as a single frame of energies, which barely change along the swing. For a camera started at release, the setting of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, angle frames are the natural choice, and v2 uses them.

\subsection{Why we moved away from the recurrent network}
\label{sec:arch}

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \input{fig_schematic}
  \caption{The two networks. (a)~v1 applies four convolutions to each frame separately, so each feature sees nine neighbouring pendulums of one frame; space and time first meet in the bidirectional LSTM, after every frame has been flattened into 25,600 numbers, each tied to a particular pendulum. (b)~v2 stacks the ten angle frames as channels of a signal on the ring, so every kernel sees all frames at once; seven circular convolutions with growing dilation let every pendulum see the whole ring, and the same small head scores every pendulum.}
  \label{fig:schematic}
\end{figure}

We now turn to the network itself. The v1 network [Fig.~\ref{fig:schematic}(a)] follows a design common for video: convolutions extract features from each frame separately, and a recurrent network then models how the features evolve from frame to frame. This is a sensible default when little is known about the dynamics. In light of Sec.~\ref{sec:floquet}, however, it seemed less suited to this problem. First, there is little temporal dynamics to model, since over the ten frames the perturbation grows by less than a factor of two and moves by about two pendulums. Second, each convolutional feature sees only nine neighbouring pendulums, whereas the growing modes span the whole ring, so the global view is left to the LSTM, whose input is each frame flattened into 25,600 numbers. The weights that read this input hold 26.2 of v1's 26.5 million parameters, and each of them is tied to a particular pendulum, so the network must learn the same physics separately at each of the 100 positions, although the ring looks the same from every pendulum. Third, the convolutions pad the ends of the chain with zeros, so that no convolution links the first and the last pendulum, although on the ring they are neighbours. Bidirectionality, finally, was motivated in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} by learning both past and future contexts; but the network makes one prediction from the whole window, so the backward pass sees nothing that the forward pass does not, while it doubles the largest block of parameters.

This suggested the alternative of Fig.~\ref{fig:schematic}(b). If the ten frames are stacked as input channels, every kernel sees all of them at once, and we hypothesized that no recurrent layer would then be needed. We further expected that each pendulum's score should depend on the whole ring, that circular padding should replace zero padding, and that an output head applying the same small network at every pendulum, one score per site, should replace the flatten and dense layers. Each of these was tested separately, with v1's inputs and the same training budget.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig4_ring.pdf}
  \caption{(a)~Mean test distance of a dilated circular CNN against its receptive field; the line is the 200-parameter linear ring filter. (b)~Mean test distance against the number of training runs for the two-branch network described in the text (shallow circular convolutions plus a global branch on the lowest ring modes) with one score per site, the same with zero padding, and with a v1-style flatten and dense head; the diamond is the rebuilt v1, trained on 60,000 runs. Zero padding costs far less here than in the final model (Table~\ref{tab:choices}), presumably because the global branch is periodic whatever the padding.}
  \label{fig:ring}
\end{figure}

The receptive field, the stretch of the ring on which a pendulum's score depends, matters most [Fig.~\ref{fig:ring}(a)]. In a circular CNN with kernels of three sites, spreading the three sites further apart from layer to layer (dilation) widens the receptive field from 9 to 129 sites, and the mean distance falls from 4.79 to 1.54. A network that sees nine pendulums, as each of v1's convolutional features does, is worse even than the linear ring filter.

Our first design reached the whole ring differently. Since the linear growth stage multiplies each ring mode by its own factor, we combined a shallow local branch of circular convolutions with a global branch that keeps only the lowest ring modes and multiplies each by a learned complex matrix that mixes the channels, a generalization of the Floquet response and the form of Fourier neural operators \cite{li2021fourier}. The two branches together beat either alone, and the global branch saturates once it includes the unstable band, as expected. The deep whole-ring CNN does better still, however, and gains nothing from the global branch, since deciding which of several growing humps wins is a nonlinear competition across the ring that no linear filter captures. The ring's symmetry, in turn, saves data [Fig.~\ref{fig:ring}(b)]. Since the dynamics are the same at every pendulum, a network that scores every site with the same filters needs to learn each pattern only once \cite{cohen2016group}; trained on 1,000 runs, the two-branch network already beats a v1-style flatten and dense head trained on 60,000.

The recurrent layer turned out to be a closer call than we had expected. On the two-branch network, convolving each frame and then passing each pendulum's ten frames through a small gated recurrent unit (GRU) \cite{cho2014learning} did help, lowering the mean distance from 1.75 with stacked frames to 1.59, and a small per-pendulum network without recurrence recovered part of this gain (1.66). In the whole-ring CNN, however, the advantage disappears. With stacked frames it scores 1.54, and with the same GRU in front 1.57. On the validation pool the whole-ring CNN, the same with the global branch, and the two-branch network with the GRU tie within one standard error, and we chose the simplest of them, the whole-ring CNN without recurrence, which also trains in less than half the time of the recurrent one. Once the convolutions see the whole ring, then, the ten frames need no recurrent model.

Two further observations complete the picture. Feeding the network the field evolved by the Floquet filter as an extra input, which we expected to leave it only the nonlinear correction to learn and so to help most when data are scarce, did not help even with 3,000 training runs; the network learns the linear growth stage from the data alone. Nor does the network need to be large. Models from 2,000 to 115,000 parameters all land within about a third of a site of each other, as one would expect if the answer lives in about ten numbers plus local texture. We also considered, but did not pursue, other families of models: on a ring with nearest-neighbour coupling a graph network reduces to a one-dimensional convolution, a transformer over sites lacks the locality of the coupling and needs much data to learn what five modes encode, and reservoir computing \cite{Chaos_Ott_2017,PhysRevLett_Ott_2018} forecasts trajectories rather than a single outcome.

\subsection{Loss and optimizer}
\label{sec:loss}

The v1 network was trained with plain cross-entropy over the 100 sites, which counts a prediction one site off as just as wrong as one 50 sites off, together with a binary head that predicts whether the run localizes at all. Since neighbouring sites are nearly equivalent at the level of the label (Sec.~\ref{sec:pools}), we expected soft labels that also credit the neighbours of the true site \cite{szegedy2016rethinking} to help, and they did, lowering the mean distance in screening runs from 1.75 to 1.58 and cutting the spread between seeds fourfold; against our expectation, however, they also lower the share of exact hits (from 41\% to 28\% at the full budget). Adding the expected ring distance to the loss, so that the network optimizes the metric we report, did not help further, and at larger weights it made the model hedge; we kept a small weight. Regressing a position on the ring did worst, as expected, because when two humps compete it averages them into a site between the two. The binary head adds nothing, since every run in our data localizes.

Since the same growing modes set both when and where the energy localizes, we also expected a head that predicts the localization time to help with the site, and it did, slightly. Whether the timing is worth predicting for its own sake is another matter. We suspected that it mostly follows simple trends in the parameters, since a larger swing makes the unstable modes grow faster, and this turned out to be largely true (Sec.~\ref{sec:final}). The optimizer, finally, is a question the physics does not answer, and indeed every adaptive optimizer and learning-rate schedule we tried landed within the spread between seeds. We kept AdamW \cite{loshchilov2019decoupled} with a cosine schedule \cite{loshchilov2017sgdr}; v1's Adam \cite{kingma2015adam} at a constant rate does about as well.

\subsection{The final model}
\label{sec:final}

The final model combines the best choices [Fig.~\ref{fig:schematic}(b)]. The ten angle frames at $\tau=0,0.5,\dots,4.5$, the observation window of v1, enter as channels of a signal on the ring. Seven circular convolutions with kernels of three sites, dilations 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 1 \cite{yu2016multiscale,oord2016wavenet} and 32 channels give every pendulum a receptive field of 129 sites, more than the whole ring. A small head, the same at every pendulum, gives a score $s_n$ per site and the probability $p_n=e^{s_n}/\sum_{n'}e^{s_{n'}}$, and a second head, linear in the ring-averaged features, predicts the logarithm of the localization time $\tau_{\mathrm{loc}}$. With $y$ the true site, the loss is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:loss}
\mathcal{L} = -\sum_n q_n\ln p_n + \lambda_d\sum_n p_n\, d(n,y) + \lambda_t\left(\hat\ell-\ell\right)^2,
\qquad q_n\propto\exp\!\left[-\frac{d(n,y)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right],
\end{equation}
that is, cross-entropy against soft labels of width $\sigma=1$ site, plus $\lambda_d=0.1$ times the expected ring distance, plus $\lambda_t=0.1$ times the squared error of the predicted log-time $\hat\ell$, where $\ell$ is $\ln\tau_{\mathrm{loc}}$ standardized over the training pool. The model has 22,786 parameters, none of them tied to a particular pendulum, and trains in about six minutes on the same 60,000 runs as v1.

Table~\ref{tab:headline} compares it with v1 and the baselines. Against the rebuilt v1, v2 halves the mean distance, from 3.14 to 1.49, cuts the far misses from 5.7\% to 1.5\%, and raises the share within $\pm1$ from 60\% to 77\%. It does so with about a thousandth of the parameters and a quarter of the training time, and all five v2 seeds trained successfully, whereas one of three v1 seeds stayed at chance level. Yet v2 does not reach the 94.4\% within $\pm1$ reported in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, a point we return to in Sec.~\ref{sec:repro}.

We then retrained the final model with one choice reverted at a time, and Table~\ref{tab:choices} pairs each choice with the reason it was made. The three architectural choices that the ring's physics dictates matter most. Seeing the whole ring is worth 1.1 sites, circular padding 0.9, and one score per site 0.3, the last with a tenth of the parameters of a dense head. Once the architecture is right, v1's inputs and optimizer cost little. The loss matters mainly for the share within $\pm1$: with plain cross-entropy that share falls from 77\% to 64\%, for a reason we shall see in Sec.~\ref{sec:target}.

The network is also economical with data: trained on only 1,000 runs, v2 already beats the rebuilt v1 trained on 60,000 (2.42 against 3.14). Nor does it need much explicit regularization. Because no parameter is tied to a particular pendulum, it does nearly as well on the test pool as on its training runs (1.49 against 1.35) with no dropout \cite{srivastava2014dropout} and only a small weight decay, whereas the rebuilt v1 overfits despite dropout and early stopping (3.00 against 1.62 for one seed). Where v2 does overfit, with little data, dropout makes it worse and weight decay up to $10^{-1}$ changes nothing. What helps is the mirror images of the training runs, the one symmetry of the ring that the network does not build in: they are worth about twice the data, and they slow the overfitting enough for a weight decay of 1 to act.

Finally, the time head predicts the localization time to a median error of 1.5\%, but most of the timing is a trend in the amplitude, which alone predicts it to 5.0\%; the remaining gain is only about two time units. As we suspected, and as the amplitude dependence of the localization time in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} already suggested, \emph{when} the energy localizes is largely set by the amplitude, whereas \emph{where} it localizes is the real prediction problem.

\subsection{One pendulum or a hump?}
\label{sec:target}

Most of v2's remaining error on the first-crossing label turns out to belong to the label. Within one swing, the energy of a forming hotspot moves back and forth between a pendulum's motion and the springs on either side of it, so which pendulum first crosses 10\% depends on the moment in the swing at which the threshold is passed. To remove this exchange, we define a \emph{swing-averaged label}: we split each spring's energy evenly between the two pendulums it joins, which gives a symmetric site energy $E^{\mathrm{s}}_n$, and average it over the last 16 samples, about one swing,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:avg}
\bar E_n(\tau_k) = \frac{1}{16}\sum_{j=0}^{15} E^{\mathrm{s}}_n(\tau_{k-j}) ;
\end{equation}
the label is the top site at the first sample at which $\max_n\bar E_n>0.1\,\Etot$. The two labels agree exactly in only a third of the test runs, the averaged one usually sitting one to three sites to the left [Fig.~\ref{fig:jitter}(a)]. The jitter shows up in the errors, too. Trained with plain cross-entropy, v2 misses by two sites more often than by one, and half of those two-site misses sit exactly on the swing-averaged position [Fig.~\ref{fig:jitter}(b)]. Soft labels hedge between the two candidate sites, which is why they raise the share within $\pm1$ so much.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig5_jitter.pdf}
  \caption{(a)~Swing-averaged site minus first-crossing site on the test pool. (b)~Prediction errors of v2 trained with plain cross-entropy and of the final model (soft labels), both on the first-crossing label, and of the same recipe trained and scored on the swing-averaged label.}
  \label{fig:jitter}
\end{figure}

This raises a more basic question: is a single pendulum the right target at all? When the first-crossing label fires, the top pendulum holds 10.3\% of the energy at that instant but only 5.5\% averaged over a swing, and the swing-averaged hump is about eight pendulums wide at half height. The 10\% on a single pendulum is thus the instantaneous peak of a breathing hump. The hump stays in place for about a swing after it forms, then drifts. In about one run in six a rival hump at least five sites away holds at least half as much energy, so that any single-site answer is a guess between two places. We therefore also define the event at the scale of the hump. The \emph{hump label} fires at the first sample at which
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:hump}
\max_n H_n > 0.15\,\Etot , \qquad H_n = \bar E_{n-1} + \bar E_n + \bar E_{n+1} ,
\end{equation}
and names the centre of that three-pendulum window. With a threshold of 15\% it fires together with the first-crossing label, at a median of 54.5 against 55 time units, whereas the swing-averaged label fires about five time units later.

\begin{table}[t]
  \centering
  \caption{The same recipe trained and scored on each label (test pool; seeds in brackets). Accuracies in \%.}
  \label{tab:labels}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}llrrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    Model & Label [seeds] & Mean dist. & Exact & $\pm1$ & $>10$ off \\
    \midrule
    v2 & First crossing [5] & 1.49 & 27.7 & 77.2 & 1.5 \\
    v2 & Swing-averaged [3] & 0.58 & 70.5 & 96.4 & 0.7 \\
    v2 & \textbf{Hump [3]} & \textbf{0.27} & \textbf{84.7} & \textbf{99.4} & \textbf{0.4} \\
    \midrule
    v1 rebuilt & First crossing [2] & 3.14 & 22.5 & 60.4 & 5.7 \\
    v1 rebuilt & Swing-averaged [2] & 2.25 & 42.0 & 83.6 & 4.4 \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

We trained and scored the same recipe on each label (Table~\ref{tab:labels}). On the swing-averaged label v2 reaches a mean distance of 0.58, with 96.4\% within $\pm1$, and on the hump label 0.27, with 99.4\%. Sharing the springs evenly without averaging over a swing does not help, so the jitter comes from the energy moving within each swing, not from how the spring energy is assigned. The hump label's further gain over the swing-averaged label comes about equally from being read when the hump forms and from naming the centre of a three-pendulum window rather than the top pendulum. The first 4.5 time units thus decide where the hump forms: even the model trained on the first-crossing label is within $\pm1$ of the hump label in 91\% of runs.

Since every design choice of Secs.~\ref{sec:inputs}--\ref{sec:loss} was made on the jittery first-crossing label, we repeated the key ones on the cleaner labels. They hold, and seeing the whole ring matters even more: with a four-layer stack that sees only 17 sites the mean distance triples on the swing-averaged label and grows more than fivefold on the hump label, against 1.6-fold on the first-crossing label. Soft labels, by contrast, stop mattering, and on the hump label plain cross-entropy does slightly better; on a label that does not jitter, the hedge only blurs the answer. The target is therefore best framed as the centre of the hump when it forms, with a probability over all pendulums as output.

\subsection{Toward a real chain}
\label{sec:realchain}

A real chain will be observed with noisy sensors, and its parameters will be known only approximately. Since an error of $10^{-3}$~rad in the initial state already moves a quarter of the labels (Sec.~\ref{sec:physics}), let us first look at sensor noise. We trained the network on camera-like data, eight angle frames over four time units with Gaussian noise on every pendulum and frame, starting the observation at $\tau=0$, 10, 20 or 30. Watching from release, the camera does well up to about $10^{-3}$~rad and degrades beyond. Interestingly, noise first causes far misses: the share within $\pm1$ hardly changes at first, while the share of far misses triples. Noise picks the wrong hump before it blurs the right one.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig6_noise.pdf}
  \caption{Waiting divides the sensor noise by the growth of the unstable modes. (a)~Mean distance of the camera setup (first-crossing label) against the sensor noise $\sigma_s$ divided by the growth of the fastest mode since release, for observations starting at $\tau=0$, 10, 20 and 30; the horizontal line is the noise-free error from release. (b)~Waiting per tenfold noise for the camera in four amplitude bins, on the first-crossing and swing-averaged labels (dots, fits; bars, 95\% intervals), against the predictions from the mean growth rate of the growing modes and from the fastest mode.}
  \label{fig:noise}
\end{figure}

Waiting helps, because the growing modes rise above the sensor noise while the noise does not grow. If the fastest mode alone set the pace, each tenfold increase in sensor noise would cost $\ln10/\sigma_1$, about 20 time units of waiting, and this was our initial prediction. Figure~\ref{fig:noise} shows that waiting pays off more slowly. The camera's error depends on the noise and the start time essentially through the noise relative to the grown signal [Fig.~\ref{fig:noise}(a)], but each tenfold increase in noise costs about 25 time units, close to what the mean growth rate of the five growing modes gives rather than the fastest one. A likely reason is that white noise enters every ring mode equally, while the site depends on all the growing modes, each of which rises above the noise at its own rate. We found this rate on the first-crossing label and then wrote it down as a prediction for the swing-averaged label before running that grid: 24.8 time units predicted, 25.5 measured. Split by amplitude, the waiting cost falls as the growth rates rise [Fig.~\ref{fig:noise}(b)]. In practice, a camera ten times coarser than $10^{-3}$~rad catches up with a precise one if it starts watching about 25 time units later, which for 20~cm pendulums still leaves about 3.6~s of warning.

Fewer sensors cost less than one might fear. Tracking every second pendulum costs nothing, with or without noise, and every fourth costs little without noise. Every eighth fails, however. Its 13 sensors satisfy the Nyquist criterion for the five growing modes, which we had expected to suffice, but at release the stable modes hold about 90\% of the perturbation, and on 13 sensors they alias onto the wavenumbers of the growing ones. Putting this together, one camera tracking every second pendulum to $10^{-3}$~rad and predicting right after release scores a mean distance of 1.93 on the first-crossing label, well ahead of the rebuilt v1 with perfect data (3.14), and locates the forming hump within $\pm1$ in 96.8\% of runs. For 20~cm pendulums, $10^{-3}$~rad is 0.2~mm at the bob; we estimate, but have not tested, that one camera at 30--60 frames per second tracking markers on the bobs can reach it.

  \centering
  \caption{Models trained on the nominal chain, tested without retraining on shifted chains (pools of 5,000 runs simulated with their own true parameters; mean distance, first-crossing label), and with sensor noise added to the nominal test pool. The last column describes the growth spectrum at $A=1.75$.}
  \label{tab:robust}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lrrl@{}}
    \toprule
    Test condition & v1 rebuilt & v2 & Growth spectrum at $A=1.75$ \\
    \midrule
    Nominal chain & 3.14 & 1.49 & 5 growing modes, $\sigma_1=0.1185$ \\
    Neighbour coupling $\gt$ $\pm10\%$ & 3.26 / 3.39 & 1.97 / 1.97 & essentially unchanged \\
    Twice the initial spread & 3.62 & 1.96 & unchanged \\
    Global coupling $\htl$ $-10\%$ & 4.36 & 4.25 & $\sigma_1$ $+21\%$; 6 modes grow \\
    Global coupling $\htl$ $+10\%$ & 5.91 & 5.53 & $\sigma_1$ $-33\%$; 3 modes grow \\
    $N=80$ / $150$ pendulums & n/a & 1.31 / 6.32 & 4 / 8 modes grow \\
    One pendulum 2~mm longer & 18.9 & 22.9 & the impurity attracts the site \\

    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

The parameters of a real chain will also be off. We applied both networks, trained on the nominal chain, to shifted ones (Table~\ref{tab:robust}), and the damage again follows the Floquet spectrum. Errors that leave the spectrum essentially unchanged, in the neighbour coupling or the initial spread, cost v2 about half a site. A 10\% error in the global coupling, by contrast, changes how fast and how many modes grow, and both networks fall to 4--6 sites, which erases most of v2's lead; $\htl$ must therefore be known to a few percent, or the model trained over a range of it. Because v2 scores every site with the same filters, it also runs on rings of other sizes, which v1 cannot, although at 150 pendulums the ring outgrows its receptive field. As found in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, an impurity strongly attracts the localization. A single pendulum about 2~mm longer, whose restoring term in Eq.~(\ref{eq:eom}) is therefore 1\% weaker, pins the site within $\pm3$ of it in 92\% of runs and defeats both networks, which have never seen such a cue. Retrained on chains with one random pendulum up to 2\% weaker, v2 finds it from the motion alone, since a longer pendulum swings slightly slower, and reaches a mean distance of 1.06.

Real pendulums also lose energy, and the missing damping was the main gap we saw between our simulations and a real chain. With linear damping the uniform swing decays toward the threshold $A_c$, so a run localizes only if its perturbation has grown enough before then: at a quality factor $Q\ge1{,}000$ almost every run still localizes, at $Q\approx330$ only 71\% do, and at $Q=100$ none do, and integrating the Floquet growth rate along the decaying swing predicts the delay. Retrained on damped chains, v2 even improves with damping, to 0.84 at $Q\approx330$ on the runs that localize, because near threshold fewer and longer modes grow and the site depends less on local detail; these are not simply the easy runs, since without damping v2 does worse on them than on the rest. Here v1's binary ``localizes'' head, which has nothing to predict on undamped chains, earns its place: from the first 4.5 time units it tells whether a run will localize at all, correctly in 99.5\% of damped runs.

\section{Reproduction of the earlier network}
\label{sec:repro}

% TODO-AUTHOR-REVIEW: This section is still being discussed with the corresponding author of
% Ref. [mittal2026jand] (wording of the discrepancy; access to the original training notebook).
% Keep it neutral and within what REPORT.md (Sec. 2) supports. Do not post before agreed.
\authorreview{This section is under discussion with the corresponding author of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, including how to word the discrepancy and whether the original training code can be recovered. It states only what the rebuild shows; do not post before the wording is agreed.}

The training notebook and dataset of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} are not available to us, so we rebuilt the CNN-BiLSTM from the description in Sec.~2.3 and the Appendix of that paper, keeping the defaults of the TensorFlow (Keras) layers it names. Its data come from a simulator that gives the same localization site and time as the original simulation code on 1,000 of 1,000 test runs, and the only deliberate change is that the input scaler is fitted on the training pool alone. We have not been able to reproduce the accuracy reported in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} from this description. Two seeds of the rebuild reach 61.7\% and 59.1\% within $\pm1$, against the published 94.4\%, and mean distances of 3.00 and 3.27, against 1.44; a third seed never trained. Nor would a later observation obviously close the gap: a single snapshot of the energy taken near the typical localization time places only about 60\% of runs within $\pm1$, and later snapshots do worse, because the hotspot keeps moving after it forms.

Three explanations remain, and they cannot be distinguished without the original code: (i)~a detail of our rebuild that the description does not specify; (ii)~the original pipeline differs from its description, for example in the definition of the label or of the features; or (iii)~the original dataset contained duplicate runs, so that some test runs also appeared in training, although most test runs would need a copy there to account for the whole gap. The second explanation can be partly tested. Section~\ref{sec:target} showed that the first-crossing label jitters by one to three sites within a swing, while the swing-averaged position does not. Trained and scored on the swing-averaged label, the rebuild reaches 83.6\% within $\pm1$ (Table~\ref{tab:labels}), about two-thirds of the way from 60.4\% to 94.4\%. A smoother label in the original pipeline would therefore be consistent with much of the gap, but not with all of it. Because the code that generated the training data of the published network is not available, this is a consistency check, not an identification; if that code resurfaces, the comparison should be rerun against it. Appendix~\ref{app:notes} collects the points where the published description and the simulation code of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} differ; since the rebuild follows the code, we do not expect any of them to account for the gap.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Conclusions}
\label{sec:conclusions}

In this study we revisited the prediction of where a noise-seeded type-III instability localizes energy in a sine-Gordon pendulum ring, starting this time from the physics of the instability rather than from the data. The Floquet growth spectrum of the uniform swing explains much of what was found empirically before. Only a handful of the longest ring modes grow, and this sets the optimal width of the box-car smoothing of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}. The outcome is deterministic, so prediction is limited by how precisely the initial state is measured rather than by chaos, and the coarse answer lives in the amplitudes and phases of the few growing modes.

The same spectrum guided the design of the neural predictor. Since little grows or travels during the observation window while the growing modes span the whole ring, the network needs a deep view of the whole ring, and with it the recurrent layer of v1 is not needed here. Since the dynamics are the same at every pendulum, the network should apply the same filters everywhere and score every pendulum the same way. A circular CNN built on these principles, with a thousandth of the parameters, halves the error of our rebuild of the CNN-BiLSTM, beats it with 60 times less training data, and barely overfits. To answer the question left open in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, the features that decide the localization site are largely the projections of the early state onto the few growing long waves, with local detail deciding the last site or two.

The target deserves as much care as the model. The first pendulum to hold 10\% of the energy is the instantaneous peak of a breathing hump about eight pendulums wide, and most of the remaining error on that label is its own jitter; defined at the scale of the hump, the event fires just as early and is located within $\pm1$ in 99.4\% of runs. For a real chain, sensor noise can be traded against warning time at a cost set by the mean growth rate of the unstable modes, and in simulation one camera tracking every second pendulum already beats the rebuilt v1 with perfect data.

These conclusions have limits. The comparison with v1 is against a rebuild; if the published pipeline differs from its description in a way that matters, the true gap could be smaller than reported here, although the physics baselines do not depend on the rebuild and v2 beats them too. Damping was simulated as linear, sensor noise as white, and impurities as a single lengthened pendulum, whereas a real chain will have small differences at every pendulum and correlated measurement errors. Testing the recommended setup on a bench-top chain is the natural next step.

\section{Training details}
\label{app:training}

\textit{v1, rebuilt.} Four time-distributed one-dimensional convolutions (32, 64, 128 and 256 filters, kernel 3, zero padding, ReLU), a per-frame flatten, a bidirectional LSTM with 128 units, 20\% dropout and 20\% recurrent dropout, a dense layer of 64 units, and two heads, a sigmoid ``localizes'' output and a softmax over the 100 sites. The input is the site energy at $\tau=0,0.5,\dots,4.5$ with $\theta_n(0)$ repeated in every frame. The loss is $0.5\times$ binary cross-entropy plus masked categorical cross-entropy; training uses Adam at a learning rate of $10^{-3}$ and batch size 64, with early stopping on the validation loss (patience 10, best weights restored), and takes about 23 minutes.

\textit{v2.} Hidden activations are GELUs \cite{hendrycks2016gelu}, and the per-site head is a circular convolution of kernel 3, a GELU and a $1\times1$ convolution. Training uses AdamW (learning rate $3\times10^{-3}$, weight decay $10^{-4}$) with a cosine decay and 3\% warmup, batch size 256, for 7,050 steps (30 epochs of 60,000 runs), keeping the checkpoint with the lowest validation mean distance, evaluated every 235 steps on 5,000 validation runs. The architecture comparison used the same budget. Inputs, losses and optimizers were screened with 15 epochs and three training seeds, so differences below about 0.1 sites there are within noise. The mirror image of a run maps pendulum $n$ to $N-1-n$, and its first-crossing label is the mirror image of the label computed with left-hand springs. Damping adds a term $-\gamma\dot\theta_n$ to Eq.~(\ref{eq:eom}), so that a free pendulum has quality factor $Q=1/\gamma$; every threshold is then a fraction of the energy the chain still holds.

\section{Notes on the published description of v1}
\label{app:notes}

In rebuilding the pipeline of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} we noted four points; where the text and the simulation code differ, we followed the code. (a)~All code, and Sec.~2.3 there, use $\htl=0.5$, whereas Sec.~2.1 of the journal version prints 0.05, a typographical error; with 0.05 the instability would have no threshold near $A=1.59$ and would not be of type III. (b)~The time axes of Figs.~2--5 and 7 there are sample indices ($\Delta\tau=0.5$), so localization happens at $\tau\approx57$ rather than 100, and the box-car comparison point ``$t=5$'' corresponds to $\tau=2.5$, before the end of the network's input window. (c)~The code assigns to each pendulum the spring to its right-hand neighbour, as in Eq.~(\ref{eq:energy}), whereas Eq.~(5) there assigns it the spring to its left-hand neighbour; the two conventions are mirror images and give the same statistics, but the labelled site differs in 21\% of runs. (d)~As described, the input scaler is fitted before the data are split into training and test sets, a minor leakage that the rebuild avoids.
